# CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies

Yandan Zheng Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore
Email: [yandan.zheng@ntu.edu.sg](mailto:)    Haoran Luo
Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore
Email: [haoran.luo@ntu.edu.sg](mailto:)    Xinliang Zhou
Affiliation: Stanford University
Email: [anhtuan.luu@ntu.edu.sg](mailto:)    Anh Tuan Luu
Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore
Affiliation: VinUniversity, Vietnam
Email: [xinliang.zhou@stanford.edu](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Can a language model learn better ways to reason about other people’s
minds by improving its own strategies, and are the strategies it learns
actually right? We study this with CogRSI. A grounded reader marks who
saw each event in a story and uses a short written principle to settle
disagreements between its readings. With a principle written by experts,
it beats self-consistency at the same token cost (73.1 vs. 68.7). A
self-improvement loop then writes the principle itself. It keeps an
update only if accuracy rises by a calibrated margin, and in one variant
only if it also passes counterfactual test pairs. The learned principles
transfer: on 800 BigToM pairs that no system had seen, each of them
scores higher than the expert principle. We then check what the learned
rules actually say. Each rule is translated into code and run on
thousands of small stories with known answers. Most of them (86.7%) give
a wrong answer in at least one situation they claim to cover, for
example by treating a character who is in the room as knowing what
happened even while asleep. Accuracy does not reveal which rules are
wrong, and the counterfactual test does not fix this. A strategy can
help in practice and still be wrong as a rule, so both need checking.
Our code and data are publicly available.¹¹ 1
[https://github.com/koanatakiyo/cogRSI](https://github.com/koanatakiyo/cogRSI)

^(\$\dagger\$)^(\$\dagger\$)footnotetext: Corresponding author.

## 1 Introduction

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) lets a model change its own artifacts,
such as prompts, tools or code, and keep the changes that help ([Wang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib43); [Yin et al., 2025](#bib.bib56); [Zhang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib58)). Reasoning about other minds is a hard test
for it. Theory of mind (ToM) is the clearest case: a system has to track
what each person saw, was told and believes. Benchmarks probe these
states in stories and conversations
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")),
and a skill that looks general can rest on surface cues ([Ullman,
2023](#bib.bib42); [Shapira et al., 2024](#bib.bib38)).

![Refer to caption](2611.01113v1/fig1_9pt_v4_sh.png)

Figure 1: The task: a strategy learned on one generator must track who
saw what on benchmarks it never saw.

![Refer to caption](2611.01113v1/fig2_9pt_v3_sh.png)

Figure 2: Overview. Rows: what persists, transfer, cognitive validity.
Existing self-improving and ToM methods leave them open. Our suite
measures them, and CogRSI addresses them.

Self-improving systems keep an artifact when it raises a score ([Wang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib43); [Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib60); [Agrawal
et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)). For reasoning about minds, two questions stay
open. Does what the loop learns transfer beyond the data it learned
from? And is a strategy that helps also correct? Take the rule “a
character who is in the room knows what happens”. It raises accuracy
whenever being there means seeing. It gives the wrong answer when a
character is in the room but asleep.

We study both questions with CogRSI and make three contributions. (C1) A
grounded reader. It marks who perceived each sentence or utterance,
reads the story with and without these marks, and uses a short written
principle to settle disagreements. (C2) Counterfactual-guided strategy
evolution. A loop writes that principle as a small library of rules,
each with a condition for when it applies. It keeps an update only if
accuracy rises by a calibrated margin. In one variant, the update must
also pass counterfactual pairs, two versions of a story that differ in
one fact about who could see what. (C3) A semantic audit. We check what
each learned rule says. Two independent models translate the rule into
code, and we run the code on thousands of small stories whose answers
follow from who saw or was told what. A rule is _invalid_ if both
translations give the same wrong answer on some story. In other words,
following the rule as written leads to a wrong belief in a situation it
claims to cover.

The learned strategies transfer. On 800 BigToM pairs that no system had
seen, every learned principle scores higher than the expert principle
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Evolved Strategies Transfer (RQ2) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
Yet 86.7% of the learned rules are invalid. Accuracy does not reveal
which ones, and the counterfactual gate does not change this
(§[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 What Evolved Strategies Say (RQ4) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
A self-improving system for reasoning about minds therefore needs two
checks: how its strategies behave, and what they say.

## 2 Related Work

We review the closest lines of work.
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Extended related work ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
gives more detail and a comparison table.

#### Self-improving systems.

Agents keep skills ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib43)), insights ([Zhao
et al., 2024](#bib.bib60)) or workflows ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib47)). They improve their scaffolding ([Zelikman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib57); [Yin et al., 2025](#bib.bib56); [Robeyns et al.,
2025](#bib.bib31)), design agents ([Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib18); [Zhang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib58)) and evolve prompts and code ([Fernando
et al., 2024](#bib.bib8); [Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib1); [Novikov
et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)). Recent work regularises these edits ([Wu
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib51); [Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib53)) and checks a
skill before keeping it. The check can be a replay on held-out tasks
([Shang et al., 2026](#bib.bib37)), a counterexample to the edited
assumption ([Nie et al., 2026](#bib.bib27)), or a test of the rule as a
falsifiable hypothesis ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib44)). Audits find
self-scored gains that do not hold ([Guo et al., 2026](#bib.bib15); [Xu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib54)), edits that only look like gains ([Wang
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib45)), selections that miss held-out gains ([Lin
et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)), and skill libraries that add little over
plain context ([Guan et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)). All of these checks
measure task success. We also check what an admitted rule says, against
a formal model of the domain.

#### Theory of mind and formal checks.

ToM methods take a character’s perspective by filtering or prompting
([Wilf et al., 2024](#bib.bib48); [Jung et al., 2024](#bib.bib19);
[Sarangi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Shinoda et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)).
Others track beliefs symbolically or over time ([Sclar et al.,
2023](#bib.bib35); [Hou et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)), verify belief traces
([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib52)), or use model-based inference ([Zhang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib59); [Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib21)). Training
with reinforcement learning ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)) does not
transfer ([Sarangi and Salam, 2025](#bib.bib33)). None of these methods
learns its strategy from failures. Our counterfactual pairs follow
contrast sets ([Gardner et al., 2020](#bib.bib10); [Kaushik et al.,
2020](#bib.bib20)). Translating natural language into checkable logic
follows nl2spec ([Cosler et al., 2023](#bib.bib6)), and we apply the
idea to strategies that an RSI loop has written.

## 3 Task and Evaluation

Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Benchmark details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
details the evaluation suite
(Figure [11](#A5.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ E.1 Task design ‣ Appendix E Benchmark details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).

#### Task.

A context $`c=(u_{1},\dots,u_{n})`$ is a story of sentences or a
conversation of utterances about agents $`\mathcal{A}`$. A question
$`q`$ asks about the mental state of one or more agents, and a system
answers $`\hat{y}=F(q,c)`$ in the benchmark’s format. In artifact-level
RSI, a builder model reads the current system’s failures on development
data $`\mathcal{D}`$ and proposes an artifact $`x`$. Following MedRSI
([Wu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib50)), $`x`$ is registered (kept) if its mean
accuracy gain over $`K`$ fresh trial cohorts exceeds a margin
$`\delta`$,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\textstyle\mathrm{reg}(x)\iff\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Delta A_{k}(x)>\delta.
``` |  | (1) |

All of $`\mathcal{D}`$ comes from one story generator, ExploreToM
([Sclar et al., 2025](#bib.bib34)). The loop sees no other data.

#### Three kinds of evidence.

Task accuracy comes from eight benchmarks: FANToM ([Kim et al.,
2023](#bib.bib22)), SimpleToM ([Gu et al., 2026](#bib.bib13)),
ExploreToM, Hi-ToM ([He et al., 2023](#bib.bib16)), OpenToM ([Xu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib55)), ToMBench ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)), CogToM
([Tong et al., 2026](#bib.bib41)) and BigToM ([Gandhi et al.,
2023](#bib.bib9)). The main test sample has 3,349 questions. A
confirmatory sample of 2,470 questions was drawn after every design
decision, and seven more benchmarks are used for testing only.
Behavioural validity comes from counterfactual pairs. A pair counts only
if both versions are answered right. Our own generator gives a 96-pair
gate split, the only one any loop sees, and a 320-pair evaluation split.
Its variants cover a character who watches, leaves, sleeps, is told, is
lied to or looks later. BigToM-U adds 800 independent pairs from BigToM
conditions that no system had answered. In a flip pair the agent does or
does not see a change. In a same pair the agent does or does not see an
irrelevant event. Semantic validity asks whether a learned rule is
correct
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Semantic Audit (C3) ‣ 4 Methodology: CogRSI ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
Each benchmark scores answers with its own rule, and Main is the mean
over the eight benchmarks. Differences use a paired bootstrap over
stories, resampling seeds and scenarios for the loops.

## 4 Methodology: CogRSI

![Refer to caption](2611.01113v1/fig4_9pt_v4_sh.png)

Figure 3: CogRSI. (A) RSI over procedures writes tools that export
perceptual access. (B) RSI over principles keeps a library of
conditioned strategies and admits an update only if it passes the
accuracy margin and, in the gated variant, the counterfactual gate. (C)
The reader applies the strategies at test time. The semantic audit
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Semantic Audit (C3) ‣ 4 Methodology: CogRSI ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"))
checks what the admitted strategies assert.

CogRSI has three parts: a reader, loops that write principles for it,
and an audit of what the loops write
(Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4 Methodology: CogRSI ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"),
Algorithms [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix C Algorithm details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
and [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix C Algorithm details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).

### 4.1 The Grounded Reader (C1)

One perception call per context labels each sentence or utterance with
the characters who witnessed it. It uses the perception rule of [Jung
et al. (2024)](#bib.bib19) with indexed outputs. PercepToM deletes what
a character did not see. Our reader keeps the whole story and adds who
saw what. It draws six samples at temperature 0.7, the budget of
self-consistency with $`k{=}6`$. Four samples read the annotated story,
or the questioned character’s view for conversations, and two read the
plain story. If the two readings conflict or the samples split closely,
one call picks between the two leading answers under a *principle*
$`P`$. It never overturns an answer held by five or six samples
(Proposition [3](#Thmproposition3 "Proposition 3 (Arbitration is local). ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
CogRSI uses an expert principle: *a character knows only what the story
shows them witnessing, being told, or working out from what they
themselves did*. The loops below write $`P`$ instead.

### 4.2 Counterfactual-Guided Strategy Evolution (C2)

#### Strategies.

The loop keeps a library $`L`$ of up to five rules. Each rule has the
form *When* condition*:* rule, with at most 60 words. The library fills
the principle slot of the reader. In each round the builder sees $`L`$
and up to four failures from one group of 80 new development questions.
It then proposes one change: add, revise or retire a rule. The builder
is never told what makes a rule valid. Up to four candidate changes
compete per round.

#### Calibrated registration.

The same principle varies by 2.7 points across trial cohorts of 80
questions. With four candidates per round, a 1-point margin keeps a
candidate with no real gain in 70% of rounds. We therefore set
$`\delta{=}3`$ points and also require a gain of at least zero on two of
the three cohorts.

#### Counterfactual guidance.

The gated variant also asks a candidate to keep the 96 gate pairs right.
Let $`\Delta V`$ be the change in correctly answered gate pairs and
$`\overline{\Delta A}`$ the mean accuracy gain. Then

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{reg}_{\mathrm{G}}\iff{}`$ | $`\displaystyle\big[\mathrm{reg}\wedge\Delta V\geq-3\big]`$ |  | (2) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\vee{}`$ | $`\displaystyle\big[\Delta V\geq 6\wedge\overline{\Delta A}\geq-0.5\big],`$ |  |  |

where the tolerances come from the reader’s run-to-run noise. The second
term keeps a candidate that fixes several pairs at no accuracy cost. A
*pairs-as-data* variant uses the same 192 gate items as ordinary trial
items with accuracy-only registration. It sees the same information
without the pair constraint. We also run an accuracy-only library, a
gated single principle, an accuracy-only loop with a 1-point margin that
writes one principle, and GEPA ([Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)) in
the same slot.
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 RSI over procedures ‣ Appendix C Algorithm details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
reports a loop that writes executable tools.

### 4.3 Semantic Audit (C3)

#### A formal model of access.

The audit needs a ground truth for what characters believe. We use the
account that seeing leads to knowing ([Wimmer et al.,
1988](#bib.bib49)), plus testimony. In one room, agents leave and
return, fall asleep and wake, move an object, whisper its location truly
or falsely, peek into a container, or change a visible or hidden
property of the object. An event updates the beliefs of everyone who
perceives it, and a whisper reaches only its listener. A fixed sample of
6,000 small worlds gives about 85k questions with known answers.

#### Translation and counterexamples.

Two models translate each rule into code: Llama-3.3-70B and
Qwen3.5-122B, neither of which wrote the rules. Each writes
applies(world, q) for the rule’s condition and predict(world, q) for its
answer. They are told to follow the words literally and do not know
which loop wrote the rule or whether it was kept. A *shared
counterexample* is a question where both translations give the same
answer and the formal model gives a different one. Two independent
readings then agree on what the rule says, and it is wrong. A rule is
invalid if it has a shared counterexample. It is valid if it has none
and the two translations agree on at least 80% of questions. It is
vacuous if it almost never applies and ambiguous otherwise. Finally, the
reader answers rendered counterexamples with and without the rule, to
see whether they change its behaviour.

We ask four questions. RQ1: How strong is the reader? RQ2: Do evolved
strategies transfer? RQ3: What does registration buy? RQ4: What do
evolved strategies say?

#### Setup.

The main model is Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (FP8) ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib30)).
The reader also runs on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct
([Grattafiori et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)), GLM-4.6V-Flash ([GLM-V Team,
2025](#bib.bib11)) and Qwen3.5-9B, served with vLLM ([Kwon et al.,
2023](#bib.bib24)) with thinking off. Baselines are zero-shot, chain of
thought (CoT) ([Kojima et al., 2022](#bib.bib23)), self-consistency (SC)
([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib46)) with $`k{=}6`$ and with $`k{=}9`$ (the
reader’s token budget), retrieval, prompt-only GEPA, SimToM ([Wilf
et al., 2024](#bib.bib48)) and PercepToM ([Jung et al.,
2024](#bib.bib19)). SimToM and PercepToM also run with our six samples.
Each loop runs eight rounds on ExploreToM development data. Every
experiment after the design freeze was pre-registered with its
hypotheses and thresholds
(Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Validity-aware RSI: details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")),
and we report every outcome.

### 5.1 The Reader (RQ1)

With the expert principle, CogRSI scores 73.1 Main, against 68.7 for SC
($`k{=}9`$) at the same token cost
(Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Each part adds, at equal cost. ‣ 5.1 The Reader (RQ1) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
It scores 73.5 against 68.5 on the confirmatory sample and beats SC
($`k{=}9`$) on all five backbones. FANToM and SimpleToM carry 81% of the
gain. On the seven test-only benchmarks it scores 65.2, against 66.2 for
SC ($`k{=}9`$). Inside the same reader, our annotated view beats
PercepToM’s filtered view by +1.3 narrative Main points (\[+0.7, +2.0\])
and SimToM’s view by +0.9 (\[+0.1, +1.7\]). With learned principles, the
reader scores 71.8–71.9 Main
(Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).

#### Each part adds, at equal cost.

The expert principle adds +3.0 Main points over no principle (\[+2.2,
+3.7\]). Even without a principle, the reader beats SC ($`k{=}9`$) by
+1.5 (\[+0.6, +2.4\]). Each reading and each arbitration step raises
belief accuracy
(Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Setup. ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"),

CogRSI makes 7.3 calls per question and uses 1.51$`\times`$ the tokens

every other system calls a lie true. The two readings of CogRSI
disagree, and arbitration picks “false” in all three runs.

### 5.2 Evolved Strategies Transfer (RQ2)

#### Beyond the expert on independent pairs.

On BigToM-U, every learned principle scores above the expert one
(Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
The gated library reaches 96.6% pair validity, against 94.5 for the
expert principle (+2.1, \[+1.0, +3.5\]) and 94.0 with no principle
(+2.6, \[+1.4, +3.9\]). The accuracy-only library gains +2.8 over no
principle. The gain comes from flip pairs, where the agent does or does
not see the change (94.9 vs. 91.2). On same pairs every principle stays
near ceiling (98.2 vs. 97.8), so learned rules do not make the reader
see missed events where there are none. SC ($`k{=}9`$) reaches 93.0,
below the reader without a principle.

#### The gate adds nothing here.

The pre-registered primary contrast, gated minus accuracy-only library,
is $`-`$0.2 (\[$`-`$1.4, +0.8\]). Gated minus pairs-as-data is $`-`$0.1
(\[$`-`$1.1, +0.9\]). The transfer comes from evolving the principle.

#### Development gains do not reach test Main.

The accuracy-only loop’s principle beats the expert one on new
development questions in most seeds (63.8 vs. 59.7,
Figure [12](#A7.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ G.5 RSI over principles ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")),
yet it loses on test Main. A loop that writes executable tools shows the
same pattern. Its library lifts ExploreToM from 67.2 to 73.9 but leaves
FANToM flat
(Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Setup. ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")),
and inheriting it instead of rebuilding it changes FANToM All^(∗) by
+0.5 (\[$`-`$0.5, +1.5\]).

#### Limits.

On test Main the gated library trails the expert principle by $`-`$1.3
(\[$`-`$1.9, $`-`$0.6\]) and is level with the accuracy-only loop (0.0).
GEPA writes prompts of 1,838–2,383 words. They reach 84.7 on ExploreToM,
67.0 Main and 84.4 on BigToM-U. When a belief must be inferred backwards
from an action, every system stays near 68.0% pair validity (37.2% on
flip pairs), and no principle helps (+0.2, \[$`-`$2.5, +2.8\]).

### 5.3 What Registration Buys (RQ3)

| Registration          | Adm. | Prec. | Harm. | Recall | Missed |
|-----------------------|------|-------|-------|--------|--------|
| 1-pt margin           | 46   | 63.6  | 31.8  | 23.7   | 22.9   |
| 3-pt margin           | 25   | 83.3  | 16.7  | 21.7   | 29.2   |
| 3-pt + gate (single)  | 25   | 83.3  | 16.7  | 17.2   | 25.0   |
| 3-pt + gate (library) | 25   | 83.3  | 16.7  | 13.0   | 43.8   |

Table 5: Selection quality (%, development data). Every candidate scored
on 120 held-out questions. Adm.: rounds with an admission; Prec./Harm.:
admitted updates that help/hurt; Recall: helpful candidates admitted;
Missed: rounds with a helpful candidate and no admission. The calibrated
margin, not the gate, makes selection precise.

#### A calibrated margin makes admissions precise.

We scored every candidate on 120 held-out development questions. Of the
updates the 1-point loop kept, 63.6% help. With the 3-point margin,
83.3% help, with or without the gate (6 and 12 kept updates,
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.3 What Registration Buys (RQ3) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
The margin halves the share of harmful updates, from 31.8 to 16.7%, and
keeps fewer helpful ones.

#### Counterfactual items help, with or without the gate.

On the evaluation split of our own generator, the gated library keeps
96.4% of pairs right, against 91.2 for the accuracy-only library (+5.1,
\[+3.6, +6.8\]). Almost all of this gain is on one case: a character
misses a move and later looks
(Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Setup. ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
On the development gate pairs, the pairs-as-data library keeps 79.2 of
96 right and the gated library 78.7. The accuracy-only library keeps
74.8, with seeds ranging from 67 to 84. The counterfactual items carry
the gain, and the pair constraint adds little. We cannot show that the
gated library is less accurate on development (+2.7, \[$`-`$1.8, +6.6\]
against pairs-as-data).

### 5.4 What Evolved Strategies Say (RQ4)

#### Most evolved rules fail somewhere.

The principle loops proposed 573 rules. 286 are invalid: for each, there
is a story it claims to cover where following it gives the wrong answer.
44 are valid, 84 are ambiguous because the two translations disagree,
and 159 almost never apply. Among the rules the audit could decide,
86.7% (\[80.7, 92.2\]) are invalid, in every loop
(Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
In the pre-registered run, one translator hit its output limit on 253
rules. We recompiled them with a larger limit and report both sets of
verdicts (before: 165 invalid and 270 ambiguous,
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Validity-aware RSI: details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).

#### Accuracy cannot filter them.

We replayed each registration rule on the same candidates. Among the
rules a 1-point margin would keep, 84.8% are invalid. The 3-point margin
gives 89.3% and the gate 88.2%
(Figure [7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Setup. ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")a).
Valid and invalid rules have the same trial gain: $`-`$1.22 against
$`-`$1.47 points, a difference of +0.24 (\[$`-`$0.82, +1.32\],
Figure [7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Setup. ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")b).
The two gain distributions differ by only 0.16 in total variation. Any
rule that keeps candidates by trial gain then mislabels valid and
invalid rules at rates that sum to at least 0.84 ([Guo et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15)). The training data explains part of this. 116 of the
286 invalid rules fail only in situations ExploreToM never contains,
such as sleeping, private telling, lies and peeking. Invalid rules also
pile up in the libraries over rounds
(Figure [7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Setup. ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")c).
Only 3 of the 28 decided rules that pass the 3-point margin are valid.

#### What each loop kept.

Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Setup. ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
follows three loops round by round. Among kept rules the audit could
decide, the invalid ones number 14/14 for the accuracy-only loop, 5/5
for the accuracy-only library, 7/9 for the gated library and 3/4 for the
gated single principle.

#### An example.

One kept rule of a gated library reads *when a question asks whether A
believes B knows the resulting state, and B was present when the event
occurred: assume A believes B knows it*
(Box ([D](#A4.SS0.SSS0.Px10 "Rule activation (J109). ‣ Appendix D Validity-aware RSI: details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"))).
Both translations answer “yes” when B was in the room but asleep. The
formal model answers “no”, because being there is not seeing. ExploreToM
never puts a character to sleep, so no trial cohort could penalise this
rule. It also passed the gate, because none of the 96 gate pairs asks
this second-order question.

#### Counterexamples matter, but only a little.

On 1139 rendered counterexamples, the rule turns a right answer wrong in
8.6% of cases. On 176 random control stories it does so in 2.8%.

#### The conditions do not decide when a rule applies.

Removing every condition from the gated libraries changes BigToM-U pair
validity by $`-`$0.5 (\[$`-`$1.6, +0.4\]). Giving each rule another
rule’s condition changes it by $`-`$0.2 (\[$`-`$1.2, +0.7\]). The reader
treats the rules as general hints and weighs them against the story.

### 5.5 Discussion: What Does the Loop Learn?

The evolved strategies are useful, and most of them are wrong as rules.
The reader explains how both can hold. It weighs a rule against a story
in which perception is already marked. It can follow a wrong rule where
it helps and override it where the story disagrees, which fits the small
effect of counterexamples and the irrelevant conditions. A strategy
handed to another reader or a person carries the rule itself, so the
rule needs its own check. The expert principle is the opposite case. It
is correct and leads on test Main, where conversations dominate, but it
loses on BigToM-U, where seeing a change is the whole question. The loop
has learned behaviour that helps this reader, and it has written that
behaviour down as rules that do not hold on their own.

## 6 Conclusion

CogRSI evolves strategies for reasoning about other minds. The evolved
strategies transfer to independent BigToM pairs, where the gated library
reaches 96.6% pair validity against 94.5% for an expert principle. A
calibrated margin raises the share of helpful updates from 63.6% to
83.3%. A semantic audit shows that 86.7% of the rules the loops propose
give a wrong answer in some situation they claim to cover. Neither
accuracy nor counterfactual gating catches this. Self-improving systems
that reason about minds should check both what their strategies do and
what they say, and using the audit during registration is the natural
next step. Our replay suggests that few current candidates would pass,
which moves the bottleneck from selecting strategies to proposing
correct ones.

## Limitations

- •
  All loops learn from one story generator. The formal model covers
  physical access and testimony in one room, and other mental states are
  left for future work.
- •
  The audit relies on two models translating rules into code. Shared
  counterexamples guard against a single mistranslation, and both
  translations can still miss what a rule’s author meant.
- •
  Loops run three to six seeds, and some arms were not evaluated on
  every test set
  (Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
- •
  All benchmarks are in English and mostly synthetic.

## Ethics, AI-Use and Reproducibility Statements

#### Ethics.

Systems that infer what a person knows or believes could be used to
profile real people from their conversations. We use only fictional
stories and synthetic dialogues and train no models.

#### Use of AI assistants.

AI assistants helped write and review code, run the experiments, and
draft and edit text. The authors directed and checked this work and are
responsible for all content.

#### Reproducibility.

Our repository contains the code, prompts, sample manifests, frozen
configurations and the scripts that generate every table, figure and
number from the per-run outputs.

## Appendix B Proofs

###### Proposition 1 (Access determines location beliefs).

If agents perceive exactly the events at their location and $`\alpha`$
is correct, an agent’s first-order belief about an object’s location is
the location set by the last move of the object in the agent’s
perspective view.

###### Proof.

Let $`o`$ change location only through units that place it (an initial
description or a move), and let agents perceive exactly the units at
their location, with no communication. Write $`V_{a}`$ for agent $`a`$’s
perspective view. By induction over $`t`$, after units
$`u_{1},\dots,u_{t}`$, $`a`$’s belief about $`o`$ is the location set by
the last placing unit in $`V_{a}\cap\{u_{1},\dots,u_{t}\}`$ (undefined
if there is none). For $`t=0`$ there is no belief. Step $`t\to t{+}1`$:
if $`u_{t+1}\notin V_{a}`$, $`a`$ did not perceive it ($`\alpha`$ is
correct), so $`a`$’s belief is unchanged, and so is the last placing
unit in $`a`$’s view. If $`u_{t+1}\in V_{a}`$ places $`o`$, $`a`$
perceives the placement and believes it, which is the new last placing
unit in $`V_{a}`$; if it does not place $`o`$, neither side changes.
Second-order questions use the chain view; this matches second-order
beliefs when co-present agents know of each other’s presence, as
ExploreToM’s generator assumes. ∎

###### Proposition 2 (Registration only climbs).

Along a seed of the principle loop, every admitted principle beats the
incumbent it replaces by more than $`\delta`$ in mean accuracy on the
$`K`$ trial cohorts of its round, and the reader changes only when a
principle is admitted.

###### Proof.

In each round every candidate $`x`$ and the incumbent $`P`$ answer the
same $`K`$ trial cohorts, and $`\Delta A_{k}(x)`$ is the accuracy of
$`x`$ minus that of $`P`$ on cohort $`k`$. By
Eq. [1](#S3.E1 "In Task. ‣ 3 Task and Evaluation ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
the candidate with the largest mean gain replaces $`P`$ only if that
mean exceeds $`\delta`$. If none is admitted, $`P`$ is kept, and the
reader, which depends on the loop only through $`P`$, is unchanged. The
bound holds on the trial cohorts, not on the population; the final
cohort
(Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 RSI over principles ‣ Appendix C Algorithm details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"))
checks the last incumbent on new questions (from stories the loop had
seen). ∎

###### Proposition 3 (Arbitration is local).

CogRSI’s answer differs from the vote over its six samples only on view
conflicts and close splits; it never overturns an answer held by five or
six samples and always returns a sampled answer. Hence arbitration
changes accuracy by at most the share of arbitrated questions.

###### Proof.

The answer equals the vote unless an arbitration call is made and its
choice is accepted; a call is made only on a view conflict or a close
split, and a choice is accepted only if it equals one of the two answers
put to the arbiter, both sampled. Suppose $`Y`$ holds at least five of
six votes. The runner-up has at most one vote, so there is no close
split. A view conflict needs both plain samples to agree and the
annotated majority to differ: if they agree on $`Y`$, at least three of
the four annotated samples are $`Y`$, so the annotated majority is
$`Y`$; if they agree on another answer, that answer has two votes and
$`Y`$ at most four, a contradiction. So no call is made, and accuracy
differs from the vote’s only on arbitrated questions. ∎

## Appendix C Algorithm details

0:  development pool $`\mathcal{D}`$, builder $`B`$, system $`S_{0}`$
(empty library or $`P=\emptyset`$), rounds $`R`$, $`K`$, $`\delta`$

1:  for $`r=0,\dots,R-1`$ do

2:   draw a discovery cohort and $`K`$ trial cohorts $`T_{1}..T_{K}`$
from unused stories of $`\mathcal{D}`$

3:   $`F\leftarrow`$ failures of $`S_{r}`$ on the discovery cohort
(Stage 2: grouped by question type $`\times`$ belief order)

4:   $`X\leftarrow B(F)`$; drop candidates that break the interface
(Stage 1) or name shown characters (Stage 2)

5:   for all $`x\in X`$ do

6:
   $`g(x)\leftarrow\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k}\mathrm{acc}(S_{r}\oplus x,T_{k})-\mathrm{acc}(S_{r},T_{k})`$
(Eq. [1](#S3.E1 "In Task. ‣ 3 Task and Evaluation ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"))

7:   end for

8:   $`x^{*}\leftarrow\arg\max_{x}g(x)`$

9:   if $`g(x^{*})>\delta`$ then

10:    $`S_{r+1}\leftarrow S_{r}\oplus x^{*}`$ (Stage 1 arm A: add the
tool; Stage 2: replace $`P`$)

11:   else

12:    $`S_{r+1}\leftarrow S_{r}`$

13:   end if

14:  end for

15:  return $`S_{R}`$ (arm C: rebuild once from round-0 failures pooled
over $`\mathcal{D}`$, same budget)

Algorithm 1 Artifact-level RSI (Stages 1 and 2)

0:  context $`c`$, question $`q`$, principle $`P`$

1:  $`\alpha\leftarrow`$ Perceive$`(c)`$ (who witnessed each unit; one
call per context)

2:  if $`c`$ is a conversation and $`q`$ asks a named chain’s belief
then

3:   $`v\leftarrow`$ perspective view of the chain

4:  else

5:   $`v\leftarrow`$ $`c`$ annotated with $`\alpha`$

6:  end if

7:  $`Y\leftarrow`$ four samples on $`(v,P)`$ and two on $`c`$
(temperature 0.7; concise retry)

8:  $`\hat{y}\leftarrow`$ majority of $`Y`$

9:  if view conflict, or close split (top $`\leq 4/6`$, runner-up
$`\geq 2/6`$; narratives) then

10:   $`y^{\prime}\leftarrow`$ Arbitrate$`(c,\alpha,`$ top two
answers$`,P)`$; if $`y^{\prime}`$ is one of them then
$`\hat{y}\leftarrow y^{\prime}`$

11:  end if

12:  return $`\hat{y}`$

Algorithm 2 CogRSI (Stage 3), one question

### C.1 RSI over procedures

Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix C Algorithm details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
runs on the MedRSI code base ([Wu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib50)) at a
pinned commit, with the backbone as solver and builder. Each round the
builder reads prioritised failures of the current solver on ExploreToM
physical-access development stories (trace, gold and wrong answer) and
proposes up to four tools; tools that fail to load or to export the
interface are discarded. A candidate is admitted if it improves a
discovery cohort and, by at least one point on average, three trial
cohorts of 40 stories.

### C.2 RSI over principles

Development data: ExploreToM e1_dev (29,752 questions over 2,519 stories
in 2,189 structural groups; the sampler draws by story), disjoint from
every test sample. Every cohort takes one question from each of a set of
unused stories: per round a discovery cohort of 80 and three trial
cohorts of 80; after eight rounds a final cohort of 300 compares no
principle, the hand-written principle of CogRSI and the loop’s
principle. Eight rounds and the final cohort need more stories than the
pool holds: once every story has been used, a new pass reshuffles the
stories and takes from each a question not used before. Seeds 0–2 ran
the first seven rounds before this rule existed and were resumed from
their saved rounds with it, which reproduces their earlier draws
exactly; later seeds used it from the start. Builder: the backbone at
temperature 0.7; one call per failure group (the four largest groups, up
to four failures each), replying with a one-sentence diagnosis and a
principle of at most 80 words that must not name the shown stories’
characters or places (checked against the perception call’s names and
capitalised words; violators and principles over 120 words are
rejected). Test runs use the frozen CogRSI runner with its two texts
replaced by the seed’s principle
(Box ([C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 RSI over principles ‣ Appendix C Algorithm details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"))).

one per seed, verbatim.

### C.3 CogRSI: reading and design history

Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix C Algorithm details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
gives the reader. Ties in the vote are broken by the first sampled
answer; samples that hit the 1,024-token cap are retried once with a
concise instruction. CogRSI was built in three steps, each frozen and
then tested on every test set
(Table [8](#A3.T8 "Table 8 ‣ C.3 CogRSI: reading and design history ‣ Appendix C Algorithm details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")):
a vote over the annotated and plain views (frozen at commit 6035943),
the arbitration of view conflicts (c86b903) and the arbitration of close
splits (e59dcbb). The first two were frozen before any of their test
results were seen. The third was developed afterwards on development
data only (held-out sample 1 and development samples of four further ToM
benchmarks) after inspecting the second design’s test failures for
diagnosis; six candidates were tried and five rejected on development
data:

- •
  Access gate: plain sampling when the perception call finds no access
  asymmetry. Development: held-out-1 narrative items: 79.7 / 78.9
  (classifier) vs 80.0 for the base design.
- •
  Construct router: emotion and non-literal questions answered from
  plain samples. Development: held-out-1: 80.0, equal to the base
  design.
- •
  Last-witnessed trace: explicit trace of what each character last
  witnessed. Development: Hi-ToM 44.2 vs 66.4 for the base design.
- •
  Extra voters: zero-shot, RSI-library and SC answers added to the vote.
  Development: lower than the base design on most development datasets.
- •
  Conflict-only gate: plain reading on conflicts the classifier deems
  access-free. Development: held-out-1: 80.4 vs 81.2 for the base
  design.

The adopted change applies the existing arbitration call, unchanged, to
every remaining close split
(Table [7](#A3.T7 "Table 7 ‣ C.3 CogRSI: reading and design history ‣ Appendix C Algorithm details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"));
it was frozen with byte-identical source checks, run once on all test
data, and every variant was re-run on the confirmatory sample
(Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Each part adds, at equal cost. ‣ 5.1 The Reader (RQ1) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")B).

## Appendix D Validity-aware RSI: details

#### Pre-registration.

Every experiment in this section was registered before its first output
(files configs/prereg_J099–J104 in our repository) with its arms, seeds,
thresholds, hypotheses and failure handling. For the principle arms the
primary hypothesis H1 is CogRSI’s library minus the accuracy-only loop
on test Main. The secondary hypotheses, Holm-corrected together, are the
library against the hand-written principle (H2), the library minus the
accuracy-only library on held-out pair validity (H3), the library minus
the single principle (H4) and the library minus GEPA (H5), the last two
on test Main. All outcomes are reported, and no arm was rerun or
extended after its outputs existed. Two test cells failed on a
connection error and were rerun with identical inputs, as the
registration allows. No seed was missing at the cutoff.

#### Loop settings.

All principle arms use the frozen reader and backbone and ExploreToM
development data only: eight rounds, a discovery cohort of 80 new
questions, three trial cohorts of 80, up to four candidates per round
and a final cohort of 300 unseen questions shared by every comparison of
a seed. The builder answers in JSON with a diagnosis, an operation (add,
revise, retire), an entry number, a condition and a rule. The library is
composed as a numbered list, “($`i`$) When condition: rule”, into both
principle positions of the reader. Among admissible candidates the
largest mean accuracy gain wins, with ties broken by the larger gate
gain. GEPA ([Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)) optimises the same slot
from an empty seed, with the reader as its metric, the reader’s failures
with gold answers as its reflective data, and 10,240 reader evaluations;
it selects on its own validation split of development questions, so its
development accuracy is not comparable and
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
omits it.

#### Counterfactual pairs.

Narratives follow ToMi’s numbered-sentence format: two characters, an
object in a container, and a move. Conversations are group chats in
which one speaker makes a claim. Each pair varies one access fact.
Narrative flip pairs are watch/leave, watch/asleep, told/leave,
look/leave, told/lied and look/lied, and narrative same pairs
leave/asleep and watch/told. Dialogue flip pairs are hear/away,
hear/muted, relayed/away and relayed/misled, and dialogue same pairs
away/muted and hear/relayed. Gold answers are computed by rule from the
access facts. The gate split has 48 narrative and 48 dialogue pairs and
the evaluation split 160 of each, drawn with different seeds from
disjoint name, place, object and template lists. In the look variant the
character who missed the move returns and checks the new container, so
the right answer is the object’s true location.
Table [9](#A4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Rule activation (J109). ‣ Appendix D Validity-aware RSI: details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
gives every arm by benchmark and by variant.

#### Registration noise.

The margin was set from development logs of the accuracy-only loop only.
A fixed principle’s accuracy varies by 2.7 points across trial cohorts
of 80 questions. Simulating four candidates with no real gain per round,
a 1-point margin admits one in 70% of rounds and a 3-point margin in
about 10%. The gate tolerances come from the reader’s run-to-run
variation in valid pairs on the counterfactual items.

#### Selection quality.

For each finished loop we scored every candidate that reached
registration, admitted or not, and its incumbent on the first 120
questions of the loop’s final cohort, which no registration step saw. A
candidate helps if it beats its incumbent there. The accuracy-only loop
proposed 192 scored candidates in 48 rounds and admitted 22. CogRSI’s
library proposed 191 and admitted 12, and the accuracy-only library and
the single principle admitted 6 and 6 of 94 and 96. The selection gap,
the best candidate’s held-out gain minus the admitted one’s, averages
1.1, 0.8, 1.0 and 1.8 points in the order of
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.3 What Registration Buys (RQ3) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies").
With so few admissions per arm the precision estimates are coarse.

#### Matched inheritance.

Arm M runs the procedure loop with A’s inheritance (its builder sees and
composes registered tools, which persist) and C’s evidence (failures of
the round-0 solver), for seeds 0–2 on the same pool and schedule. On the
full sealed FANToM set, with the seed-paired bootstrap of the original
comparison, M $`-`$ C is +0.5 points (95% CI \[$`-`$0.5, +1.5\]; the 90%
interval lies within the pre-registered 3-point equivalence margin), A
$`-`$ C +0.6 (\[$`-`$2.0, +4.1\]) and M $`-`$ A $`-`$0.2 (\[$`-`$3.1,
+2.2\]). Inheritance makes no meaningful difference, whichever evidence
the builder sees.

#### Controlled reader.

To separate the view from the rest of the reader, we replaced the
annotated story with PercepToM’s filtered story or SimToM’s
perspective-taking story and kept perception, sampling, voting,
arbitration and the hand-written principle fixed. On the narrative
benchmarks of the main test sample the annotated view beats the filtered
view by +1.3 Main points (\[+0.7, +2.0\]) and the perspective view by
+0.9 (\[+0.1, +1.7\]). The largest gaps are on Hi-ToM (+6.3 and +3.7),
where the filters drop context that higher-order questions need.

#### Semantic audit (J105).

The oracle (src/cogrsi/access_oracle.py) samples worlds event by event
from the legal moves: leave, enter, fall asleep, wake, move the object,
whisper a location to one listener (true or false), peek into the
container that holds the object, or change a visible or hidden property.
Moves and changes are perceived by the agents present and awake and by
the actor; a whisper by its speaker and listener; a peek by the peeker;
a visible property also by anyone who later enters or wakes while the
object is in view. Second-order beliefs change only through events both
agents perceive, or when one tells the other. The audited population is
every candidate that reached registration in the accuracy-only loop, the
accuracy-only library, the gated library and the gated single principle
(573 texts; the entry an add or revise writes, or a whole single
principle). The compilers see only the rule text. Before the freeze,
three hand-written rules were used to fix the sandbox, the compile
instructions, a deterministic scope guard for second-order questions,
private telling and peeking, and the shared-counterexample criterion.
The pre-registered run gave 165 invalid, 29 valid, 270 ambiguous and 109
vacuous texts; 253 of the ambiguous ones had no code because the
Qwen3.5-122B replies hit the 2,048-token output cap. A recorded
deviation recompiled those texts with an 8,192-token cap and nothing
else changed (43 still hit it), giving 286, 44, 84 and 159. Shadow
registration replays each candidate under each rule against its own
incumbent and logged trial gains; the loops that ran without the gate
were scored on the gate pairs afterwards. Admitted rules that were
invalid, by arm: accuracy-only loop 14/14, accuracy-only library 5/5,
gated library 7/9, gated single principle 3/4. Without the rule, the
reader answers 29.4% of rendered counterexamples and 35.2% of controls
wrongly: these stories are hard in themselves.

#### Objective vs. data (J106) and transfer (J107).

Arm B (pairs as data) and seeds 3–5 of the accuracy-only library were
run with the J101 settings; their test-sample and own-pair evaluations
were not run before this version. BigToM-U uses BigToM’s conditions that
state the initial belief, with true/false-belief flip pairs and
true/false control same pairs (800 pairs from 200 scenarios); every
scenario’s other version had appeared in an earlier split, so the set is
new in its conditions and pairing, not its scenarios. On flip pairs:
gated library 94.9, accuracy-only library 95.5, pairs as data 95.1,
expert 91.2, none 90.2, SC ($`k{=}9`$) 88.5, GEPA 70.5. Backward belief
(400 pairs): gated library 68.0, accuracy-only library 68.1, expert
68.1, none 67.8.

#### Rule activation (J109).

Intact gated libraries score 96.6 on BigToM-U, 96.0 with every condition
removed and 96.3 with conditions swapped between entries (flip pairs
94.9, 93.9, 94.4).

## Appendix E Benchmark details

### E.1 Task design

A system receives a context (story or conversation) and a question in
the benchmark’s native format and returns an answer in that format; it
never sees gold answers or test items during development. The RSI loops
see only ExploreToM development stories; CogRSI’s design used held-out
sample 1.

![Refer to caption](2611.01113v1/fig3_9pt_v2_sh.png)

Figure 11: Task and suite. (A) Task. (B) Eight benchmarks. (C) Sealed,
disjoint samples. (D) Native scoring.

#### Sample construction.

Samples are drawn by story with fixed seeds and are disjoint by
construction
(Figure [11](#A5.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ E.1 Task design ‣ Appendix E Benchmark details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")C).
S0 holds the smoke subsets (never reported), S1 the development data, S2
held-out sample 1 (CogRSI’s development set), S3 held-out sample 2 (the
main test sample) and S4 held-out sample 3, drawn after every design
decision. Every design was frozen, with byte-identical source checks,
before its test runs
(Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 CogRSI: reading and design history ‣ Appendix C Algorithm details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
Two qualifications apply. Close-split arbitration was developed after
inspecting the test failures of the design without it, so main-sample
results for the final reader are exploratory and S4 is its confirmatory
test. For FANToM, SimpleToM and ExploreToM, every held-out sample, S4
included, is a subset of the sealed test sets on which the baselines and
Stage-1 libraries ran before CogRSI existed, and FANToM baseline
failures from those sets were read for diagnosis. For these three
benchmarks S4 is independent of every CogRSI design decision, not unseen
by the project.

### E.2 Construction

All inputs are text. MMToM-QA and MuMA-ToM are run in their text-only
versions (the stories and dialogues released with them; no video), and
Social-IQ 2.0 as a written description of each clip followed by its
transcript; the descriptions were written once from the clip frames by
the backbone with image input enabled for that pass only. No system sees
images or video, so these results say nothing about multimodal transfer.
Each benchmark’s test pool was sealed before the formal runs. Samples
are drawn by story, conversation or ExploreToM structural group with
fixed seeds (smoke and held-out 1: 0, held-out 2: 1, confirmatory: 3),
and each excludes every unit of the earlier ones; the confirmatory draw
is disjoint from the development data, the smoke subsets and held-out
samples 1 and 2. For FANToM, SimpleToM and ExploreToM all three held-out
samples are subsets of the sealed test sets on which the baselines and
Stage-1 libraries were evaluated on October 6–9, before CogRSI existed
(Tables [18](#A7.T18 "Table 18 ‣ G.2 Main results of the reader ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")–[24](#A7.T24 "Table 24 ‣ G.2 Main results of the reader ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")),
and FANToM baseline failures from those sets were read for diagnosis. No
CogRSI design decision used held-out sample 3, but for these three
benchmarks its independence is at the level of design decisions, not of
exposure to the project.
Table [10](#A5.T10 "Table 10 ‣ E.2 Construction ‣ Appendix E Benchmark details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
gives the sizes. ToMBench items with repeated IDs were disambiguated and
options with empty text removed before any draw.

| Benchmark     | Input        | Held-out 1 | Main test           | Confirm.  |
|---------------|--------------|------------|---------------------|-----------|
| FANToM        | conversation | 84 conv.   | 187 sets (74 conv.) | 75 conv.  |
| SimpleToM     | story        | 334 (167)  | 334 (167)           | 334 (167) |

| ExploreToM E2 | story        | 254 (51)   | 250 (50)            | 254 (51)  |

Table 10: Samples per benchmark: questions (stories or groups in
parentheses; FANToM: All^(∗) sets and conversations). Held-out sample 1
is CogRSI’s development set; the main test sample is held-out sample 2;
the confirmatory sample is held-out sample 3. SimpleToM: behavior and
judgment questions scored.

### E.3 Metrics

Accuracy is each benchmark’s own rule: option match for multiple choice,
the benchmarks’ scripts for free text and lists; FANToM uses its
official scorer on short contexts, and All^(∗) counts a target set as
right only if every question in it is right. PercepToM’s FANToM runs are
scored from their per-question results like every other system, because
the official scorer’s printed summary for those runs cannot be
reproduced from the per-question results it writes (for every other
system the two agree exactly). ATOMS constructs are mapped from each
benchmark’s question type by a fixed table; no independent annotation
validates these labels. Paired differences are bootstrapped over stories
or conversations (2,000 resamples); within-benchmark construct effects
centre each question’s difference on its benchmark’s mean.

## Appendix F Baseline details

All baselines use the backbone, decoding settings and output cap of
CogRSI
(Table [11](#A6.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Appendix F Baseline details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
Native solver: the Stage-1 solver with an empty library (floor).
Zero-shot: the question and context with the answer-format instruction.
CoT ([Kojima et al., 2022](#bib.bib23)): step-by-step reasoning before
the answer. SC ($`k{=}6`$), SC ($`k{=}9`$) ([Wang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib46)): majority over $`k`$ CoT samples at temperature 0.7,
$`k{=}6`$ being CogRSI’s number of samples and $`k{=}9`$ its tokens per
question, run by the frozen CogRSI runner with $`k`$ fixed. Retrieval:
the most similar development failures (sentence embeddings of question
and story), shown as solved examples with their correct answers. GEPA
([Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)): prompt-only optimisation on
ExploreToM development data, three optimizer seeds. SimToM ([Wilf
et al., 2024](#bib.bib48)): a first call asks which events or utterances
the target character knows about, a second answers from them with our
CoT prompt (CoT when no character is named). PercepToM ([Jung et al.,
2024](#bib.bib19)): its perception and perspective-filtering steps with
a zero-shot fallback when the target character is not found; PercepToM +
SC (belief) on FANToM: six samples over its filtered conversation for
belief questions, six plain samples otherwise, majority vote.
PercepToM + SC and SimToM + SC: CogRSI’s six samples at temperature 0.7
drawn over PercepToM’s filtered context (every question) or after
SimToM’s perspective-taking call, with SimToM’s answer prompt, majority
vote. Lib-A/C: the Stage-1 libraries, inherited and rebuilt, three loop
seeds. Not run: DEL-ToM ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib52)) needs a verifier
trained on its own simulator; AutoToM ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib59))
and ThoughtTracing ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib21)) answer through a
planning model with a different interface; Decompose-ToM ([Sarangi
et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)) and Shoes-of-Others ([Shinoda et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40)) are perspective methods of the kind SimToM and

part.

### G.1 Protocol and implementation

Every system runs the same served model per backbone through vLLM 0.30.0
(PyTorch 2.13, Transformers 5.18), thinking off, 32k context and a
1,024-token output cap
(Table [16](#A7.T16 "Table 16 ‣ G.1 Protocol and implementation ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
Each run is one execution over a sample; failed runs are retried and
reported
(Table [20](#A7.T20 "Table 20 ‣ G.2 Main results of the reader ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
Every frozen design is recorded with its commit and source hash next to
its outputs.

| Backbone | Architecture | Weights | GPUs |
|----|----|----|----|
| Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (main) | MoE, 256 experts, 40 layers | FP8 | 1$`\times`$H200 / A6000 |
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B | MoE, 256 experts, 48 layers | FP8 | 1$`\times`$H200 |
| Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct | dense, 80 layers | AWQ 4-bit | 1$`\times`$H200 / 2$`\times`$A6000 |
| GLM-4.6V-Flash | dense, 40 layers, text-only serving | BF16 | 1$`\times`$A6000 |
| Qwen3.5-9B | dense, 32 layers | BF16 | 1$`\times`$H200 / A6000 |

### G.2 Main results of the reader

1.  1.
    CogRSI is first on Main. On the main backbone it scores 73.1,
    against 68.3 for SC ($`k{=}6`$) and 68.7 for SC ($`k{=}9`$). On
    Qwen3.5-122B and Llama-3.3-70B it scores 75.6 and 72.3 against 72.1
    and 69.6, and it beats SC ($`k{=}9`$) on all five backbones at equal
    tokens
    (Table [13](#A7.T13 "Table 13 ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
2.  2.
    The margin is largest where access decides the answer. On FANToM
    All^(∗) it beats the strongest baseline by +4.3 points (95% CI
    \[+0.2, +8.6\]), on Hi-ToM by +4.4 (\[+1.2, +7.6\]), and SC
    ($`k{=}6`$) on SimpleToM by +19.9. FANToM and SimpleToM carry 81% of
    the gain over SC ($`k{=}9`$) (85% on the confirmatory sample), and
    the other six average 1.2 points, so the gain targets
    perception-dependent tasks.
3.  3.
    It holds on the confirmatory sample. On it
    (Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Each part adds, at equal cost. ‣ 5.1 The Reader (RQ1) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")B),
    CogRSI scores 73.5 (three runs, 73.1–74.2) against 68.5 for SC
    ($`k{=}9`$) (68.1–69.1), and CogRSI-L scores 72.7 over six seeds.
    The vote-only design, frozen before testing, already scores 72.0.
4.  4.
    It does not hold on seven further benchmarks. There CogRSI scores
    65.2, against 66.2 for SC ($`k{=}9`$) and 66.7 for PercepToM + SC,
    and CogRSI-L scores 64.0
    (Table [17](#A7.T17 "Table 17 ‣ G.2 Main results of the reader ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
    SimToM + SC is best on ToMi (85.6 vs. 66.0), and on the confirmatory
    items SimToM leads.

Table [19](#A7.T19 "Table 19 ‣ G.2 Main results of the reader ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")

not a test sample). Before CogRSI existed, the RSI libraries and the
baselines were evaluated on the full sealed test sets of FANToM,
SimpleToM and ExploreToM (the planned E1/E2 study, whose primary
endpoint is reported in
§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 What Registration Buys (RQ3) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"));
Tables [18](#A7.T18 "Table 18 ‣ G.2 Main results of the reader ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")–[24](#A7.T24 "Table 24 ‣ G.2 Main results of the reader ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
give those results, including appendix-only systems.
Table [20](#A7.T20 "Table 20 ‣ G.2 Main results of the reader ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
lists every run. The seven test-only benchmarks are in
Table [17](#A7.T17 "Table 17 ‣ G.2 Main results of the reader ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies").
On them CogRSI is level with self-consistency (65.2 vs. 65.3 and 66.2),
PercepToM + SC is best on average (66.7), and SimToM + SC leads on ToMi
(85.6 vs. 66.0). On the confirmatory sample’s five test-only benchmarks
the picture is the same (67.1 vs. 67.7 for SC ($`k{=}9`$) and 71.2 for
SimToM).

### G.3 Ablation study of the reader

#### What each part adds.

The rows of
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Setup. ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
compare whole systems. No Stage-1 output enters Stage 2 or 3: Stage 1
only motivated the access annotation. Lib-A scores 59.3 Main because it
lacks the whole reader. Inside the same reader, the hand-written
principle adds +3.0 Main points over no principle (95% CI \[+2.2,
+3.7\]), the loop’s principle adds +1.7 (\[+1.1, +2.3\]), and the reader
with no principle already beats SC ($`k{=}9`$) by +1.5 (\[+0.6, +2.4\]).
In Stage 3 each reading and each arbitration step lifts belief accuracy,
within the bound of
Proposition [3](#Thmproposition3 "Proposition 3 (Arbitration is local). ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies").
On FANToM All^(∗) the differences between Stage-3 variants are within
the spread of three runs
(Table [20](#A7.T20 "Table 20 ‣ G.2 Main results of the reader ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).

#### Annotating and filtering are close.

With the same arbitration, PercepToM’s filtered reading reaches 78.1 on
the main multiple-choice benchmarks and CogRSI, which keeps the whole
story, reaches 78.9. The two also differ in sample allocation, so this
small gap does not isolate annotation from filtering. With our six
samples PercepToM + SC and SimToM + SC reach 66.5 and 63.9 Main, and on
FANToM All^(∗) 3.7 and 1.8, against 28.0.

Table [12](#A7.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
gives PercepToM’s filtered reading the same arbitration as CogRSI: where
its answer and self-consistency’s differ, the evidential rule decides.
On 561 development conflicts the evidential rule is right 314 times, the
plain view 267, the annotated view 254 and a neutral arbiter 218;
without the rule the model assumes characters noticed hidden facts
(SimpleToM: 23 vs. 114 of 140;
Appendix [G.8](#A7.SS8 "G.8 Case study ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).

Strongest baseline: the highest
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Each part adds, at equal cost. ‣ 5.1 The Reader (RQ1) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
score among all baselines, including SimToM + SC and PercepToM + SC.
Holm: significant after Holm correction over the eight benchmarks
(bootstrap $`p`$-values, familywise 0.05). An interval that includes
zero is not evidence of equivalence.

On Percept-ToMi’s gold perceivers ([Jung et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)),
Lib-A’s tools export at most 10% of the gold access pairs; rebuilt tools
omit perceivers (precision 99.7, recall 42.2) or credit characters in
other rooms (74.8 / 88.5). Inheriting the library minus rebuilding it is
+0.6 points of FANToM All^(∗) (95% CI \[$`-`$7.3, +8.6\] under the
pre-registered hierarchical bootstrap over runs and conversations, and
\[$`-`$2.0, +4.1\] under the seed-paired bootstrap used for the matched
arm in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Validity-aware RSI: details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"));
acquiring communication with the inherited library in reach rather than
without it gives $`-`$1.8 (\[$`-`$6.8, +3.2\]). The inheriting runs
admitted 0–1 tools and had a non-empty library in 4 of 24 rounds; the
rebuilding runs admitted 2–5
(Table [6](#A3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ C.1 RSI over procedures ‣ Appendix C Algorithm details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).

### G.5 RSI over principles

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 12: RSI over principles. (a) Incumbent’s accuracy on new
development questions by round (mean and range over 6 seeds; round 0
admits the first principle). (b) 300 new development questions on seen
stories, per seed (no, hand-written, loop-written principle). (c) Test

#### Code and text differ in more than the artifact.

CogRSI-L scores 71.8 Main and 25.3 FANToM All^(∗), against 59.3 and 2.3
for Lib-A
(Figure [12](#A7.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ G.5 RSI over principles ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")c),
but they also differ in perception, readings, voting and arbitration. It
beats CogRSI on ExploreToM (74.0 vs. 72.5), Hi-ToM (70.0 vs. 69.3) and
OpenToM (76.5 vs. 75.8), and trails it on FANToM All^(∗) and SimpleToM
(Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Each part adds, at equal cost. ‣ 5.1 The Reader (RQ1) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).

Table [14](#A7.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
gives every seed: admitted rounds, the final development cohort and the
main test sample; near its source CogRSI-L leads CogRSI on ExploreToM
(74.0 vs. 72.5) and trails it on FANToM All^(∗) (25.3 vs. 28.0) and
SimpleToM (81.7 vs. 90.0). Trial accuracy rises by construction, since a
round is admitted only if it does. On a development cohort of new
questions, scored after every round, the incumbent goes from 56.0 (no
principle) to 62.3 after round 0 and stays between 60.2 and 62.9 after
that. The final principles score 63.2, against 59.7 for ours and 59.3
for none. On the main test sample the reader with no principle scores
70.1 Main (three runs, highest 70.3), below the lowest CogRSI-L seed
(70.9).

### G.6 Grounded reading

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 13: Grounded reading. (a) Belief and knowledge accuracy. (b)
Narrative accuracy by reading. (c) Conflicts settled correctly.
Grounding helps epistemic questions, and two readings with the
evidential rule beat one.

#### Grounding helps epistemic questions.

CogRSI is the most accurate system on belief and knowledge questions
(Figure [13](#A7.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ G.6 Grounded reading ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")a).
Pooled over benchmarks it beats SC ($`k{=}6`$) on beliefs by +3.9 points
(CI \[+2.5, +5.4\]). Within benchmarks the belief gain remains (+1.2,
\[+0.3, +2.1\]), while non-literal and mixed questions lose ($`-`$1.7
and $`-`$4.1,
Table [25](#A7.T25 "Table 25 ‣ G.4 RSI over procedures ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
Grounding helps the cognitive side of ToM, which in humans dissociates
from the affective side ([Shamay-Tsoory and Aharon-Peretz,
2007](#bib.bib36)).

#### Perception limits true belief.

With the gold perceivers of Percept-ToMi in place of the perception call
(Table [27](#A7.T27 "Table 27 ‣ Two readings, settled by the rule. ‣ G.6 Grounded reading ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")),
CogRSI rises from 60.5 to 70.3 and CogRSI-L from 63.3 to 81.0, most on
second-order true belief (2.8 to 35.4), while SC, which never calls
perception, stays near 59.8. On FANToM gold perceivers lift belief
accuracy (79.3 to 91.2) but not All^(∗) (26.0 to 25.2).

#### Two readings, settled by the rule.

The vote over both readings beats either reading alone on belief,
knowledge and all narrative questions
(Figure [13](#A7.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ G.6 Grounded reading ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")b).
On 561 development conflicts the evidential rule is right 314 times, and
an arbiter told only to choose the better answer is right 218 times. On
belief test conflicts the rule beats both readings (353 of 602,
Figure [13](#A7.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ G.6 Grounded reading ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")c),
and close-split arbitration fixes 76 answers while breaking 39.

Table [25](#A7.T25 "Table 25 ‣ G.4 RSI over procedures ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
gives every ATOMS construct. Pooled over benchmarks CogRSI improves on
SC ($`k{=}6`$) for knowledge (+1.1, \[+0.2, +2.0\]) as for beliefs;
within benchmarks only the belief gain remains, and non-literal
($`-`$1.7, \[$`-`$3.5, $`-`$0.1\]) and mixed questions ($`-`$4.1,
\[$`-`$8.4, $`-`$0.6\]) lose. Where access is irrelevant the annotations
cost accuracy (non-literal: 72.9 annotated vs. 80.5 plain; emotions:
73.1 vs. 77.2); on non-literal conflicts the plain reading is right 25
of 27 times, arbitration 16. The perception call is precise (98.2, 98.7)
but incomplete (recall 38.3, 73.8).

Gold perceivers.
Table [27](#A7.T27 "Table 27 ‣ Two readings, settled by the rule. ‣ G.6 Grounded reading ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
replaces each system’s perception call with the gold perceivers of
Percept-ToMi (576 questions) and Percept-FANToM ([Jung et al.,
2024](#bib.bib19)) (the 62 conversations of the main FANToM sample that
it annotates); everything else is unchanged. On Percept-ToMi CogRSI
rises from 60.5 to 70.3, CogRSI-L from 63.3 to 81.0 and PercepToM from
48.8 to 59.3. The largest gains are on true-belief questions, where a
character who saw the move must be counted: second order 2.8 to 35.4 for
CogRSI and 11.2 to 59.1 for CogRSI-L. PercepToM gains instead on
second-order false belief (1.9 to 72.7), where its filter must keep the
right perceivers, and loses on second-order true belief (47.2 to 19.0).
SC does not call perception and stays at 59.8/60.4. On FANToM gold
perceivers raise belief accuracy to about 91.2 for every system but
leave All^(∗) unchanged (CogRSI 26.0 to 25.2), since All^(∗) also needs
every answerability and info-accessibility question of a set right.

### G.7 Cost and robustness

#### On the cost–accuracy frontier, with a significant margin.

CogRSI makes 7.3 calls per question against 6.0 for SC ($`k{=}6`$) and
uses 1.51$`\times`$ its tokens. SC ($`k{=}9`$) uses as many and scores
lower on Main (68.7 vs. 73.1,
Figure [9](#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Each part adds, at equal cost. ‣ 5.1 The Reader (RQ1) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")a).
A Stage-1 run takes 4.3 hours on one H200. Against SC ($`k{=}9`$) the
paired 95% intervals exclude zero on FANToM, SimpleToM and Hi-ToM only,
and Hi-ToM does not survive Holm correction
(Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Each part adds, at equal cost. ‣ 5.1 The Reader (RQ1) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
Against the strongest baseline of each benchmark, CogRSI wins 2, ties 5
and loses 1, and none of these differences survives Holm correction
(Table [26](#A7.T26 "Table 26 ‣ G.4 RSI over procedures ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).
On each of the five backbones its four-benchmark mean beats SC
($`k{=}9`$) by +5.1 to +8.6 points at 0.98 to 1.15 times its tokens
(Figure [9](#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Each part adds, at equal cost. ‣ 5.1 The Reader (RQ1) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")b,
Table [13](#A7.T13 "Table 13 ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")).

### G.8 Case study

#### Arbitration breaks the tie.

On an egocentric lie from ToMBench
(Figure [10](#S5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Each part adds, at equal cost. ‣ 5.1 The Reader (RQ1) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"),
Table [28](#A7.T28 "Table 28 ‣ Arbitration breaks the tie. ‣ G.8 Case study ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")),
every run of every other system answers that Miss Zhou’s claim is true.
In CogRSI’s first run the annotated reading says false, the plain one
true, and the vote ties. Arbitration chooses false in all three runs.

[TABLE]

Table 28: Case study: a ToMBench item every baseline misses and CogRSI
gets right by arbitration.

The main case
(Table [28](#A7.T28 "Table 28 ‣ Arbitration breaks the tie. ‣ G.8 Case study ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"))
was chosen as a test item that every baseline run answers wrongly and
every CogRSI run answers correctly; the decisive step of each run is
read from its saved records. With the loop’s principles (CogRSI-L),
which are about object locations and states, all six samples agree on
the wrong answer, so no arbitration call is made. A second case, a
SimpleToM development question on which the readings disagree (held-out
sample 1): the plain samples credit Isla with knowing about the malware,
which the story never shows her learning; the annotation and the
evidential rule do not, while the neutral arbiter sides with the plain
reading.

## Appendix H Extended related work

#### Self-improving systems.

Skill and tool libraries that grow with use go back to program induction
([Ellis et al., 2021](#bib.bib7)) and embodied agents ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib43)); agents distil experience into insights ([Zhao
et al., 2024](#bib.bib60)) or workflows ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib47)), learn from verbal reflection ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib39)), improve their own scaffolding ([Zelikman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib57); [Yin et al., 2025](#bib.bib56); [Robeyns et al.,
2025](#bib.bib31)), design agents ([Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib18)), keep
an open-ended archive of self-modified agents ([Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib58)), and evolve prompts ([Fernando et al.,
2024](#bib.bib8); [Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)) or programs against
evaluators ([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)).
Table [15](#A7.T15 "Table 15 ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies")
compares what each keeps and how it admits a change; CogRSI alone
compares inheritance with a rebuild at the same budget and lets the same
loop write a principle instead of a procedure.

#### Theory of mind in language models.

SymbolicToM ([Sclar et al., 2023](#bib.bib35)) tracks beliefs in graphs,
SimToM ([Wilf et al., 2024](#bib.bib48)) answers from the events a
character knows, TimeToM ([Hou et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)) builds
temporal belief chains, PercepToM ([Jung et al., 2024](#bib.bib19))
filters the story by perception, Decompose-ToM ([Sarangi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32)) recursively simulates perspectives and
Shoes-of-Others ([Shinoda et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)) prefills the
target’s perspective; all apply a fixed procedure. DEL-ToM ([Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib52)) scores belief traces with a trained verifier, AutoToM
([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib59)) and ThoughtTracing ([Kim et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21)) infer mental states by inverting an agent model, and
[Lu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib26) train small models with reinforcement
learning, whose ToM does not generalise beyond the training datasets
([Sarangi and Salam, 2025](#bib.bib33)). Stress tests show that LLM ToM
often relies on templates ([Ullman, 2023](#bib.bib42); [Shapira et al.,
2024](#bib.bib38)); our construct analysis
(Appendix [G.6](#A7.SS6 "G.6 Grounded reading ‣ Appendix G Experiment details ‣ CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies"))
adds to this.

#### Cognitive science.

Children learn that seeing leads to knowing ([Wimmer et al.,
1988](#bib.bib49); [Pratt and Bryant, 1990](#bib.bib29)); adults track
who saw what alongside a flexible inferential system ([Apperly and
Butterfill, 2009](#bib.bib2)) and infer beliefs from actions ([Baker
et al., 2017](#bib.bib3)); cognitive and affective ToM dissociate
([Shamay-Tsoory and Aharon-Peretz, 2007](#bib.bib36)). We organise the
construct analysis by the ATOMS taxonomy ([Beaudoin et al.,
2020](#bib.bib4)).
````
